qs.q: A 40-year-old man develops progressive choreiform movements and dementia. His father had similar symptoms. Which mutation is most likely? Huntington disease (autosomal dominant, CAG repeat expansion). ---
o: Large deletion in the CFTR gene
Missense mutation in the FBN1 gene
Deleterious mutation in the TP53 gene
Trinucleotide repeat expansion in HTT gene
qs.e: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene.

qs.q: Pellagra, a disease characterized by dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia, is caused by a deficiency of which vitamin?
o: A. Vitamin B3, also known as niacin
B. Vitamin B6, known as pyridoxine
D. Vitamin C, the antioxidant ascorbic acid
qs.e: Pellagra is caused by a severe deficiency of Niacin (Vitamin B3) or its precursor, tryptophan. Niacin is a component of NAD+ and NADP+, critical coenzymes in many metabolic reactions.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Dementia is a progressive decline in cognition that interferes with daily life. It is diagnosed by history, exam, and supported by imaging and biomarkers, and managed by treating reversible causes and providing supportive care.

sections.p: Dementia is a persistent, progressive impairment of memory and other cognitive domains that causes functional decline. Diagnosis follows DSM‑5 criteria: cognitive decline >3 months, impairment in at least two domains, and functional loss.

t.b: Screen for global cognition; score <24 suggests dementia
Detect mild cognitive impairment; score <26 indicates impairment
Rule out structural lesions, vascular disease, or hydrocephalus
Support Alzheimer’s pathology; low Aβ42 and high tau suggest AD

t.a: Serum B12, TSH, RPR, HIV, hepatitis B/C

sections.p: The Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) stages dementia from 0 (no impairment) to 3 (severe). Staging guides prognosis and care planning.
In low‑resource settings, treatable causes must be excluded first. The most common causes are Alzheimer’s disease, vascular dementia, and infectious or metabolic disorders.
Patients report memory loss, confusion, and difficulty with familiar tasks. Early signs include word-finding difficulty and impaired executive function.
Use a stepwise approach: basic labs, imaging, and specific biomarkers when available. When tests are unavailable, rely on clinical judgment and simple tools.
Red flags suggest urgent evaluation or alternative diagnosis. Complications include falls, malnutrition, and delirium.
Treat reversible causes first, then provide disease‑specific therapy and supportive care. Pharmacologic options target cholinergic deficits and glutamatergic excess.
b: Regular monitoring for side effects (GI, bradycardia)

sections.p: Regular reassessment of cognition, function, and caregiver burden is essential. Prevention focuses on vascular risk control and early treatment of reversible causes.
Several conditions mimic dementia; distinguishing them is critical for appropriate treatment.
Some investigations may be falsely normal or abnormal, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: HIV serology may be negative in early infection

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid cognitive decline, new focal neurological signs, severe agitation, unexplained weight loss, or sudden worsening of symptoms

faq.q: Is normal pressure hydrocephalus a type of dementia?
faq.a: It presents with dementia, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence; it is treatable with shunting.
